title: Cognitive Load Theory
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Jamie Lee Clark opens a new DistillED series on contemporary Cognitive Load Theory by explaining it as a theory of how people learn knowledge that must be explicitly taught. The central bottleneck is that working memory can hold only a few new items for a few seconds, while long-term memory has no known limit and frees working memory once knowledge is stored there. The piece distinguishes intrinsic load, which comes from the content, from extraneous load, which comes from how it is presented, and builds the explanation around element interactivity. The chess experiments of de Groot and of Chase and Simon show that expertise is stored knowledge rather than a bigger working memory. Clark then offers a five-step planning routine: check prior knowledge, find the high-interactivity moments, match guidance to interactivity, cut extraneous load, and fade support as knowledge grows. Each step comes with a subject-specific classroom example.
points: Cognitive Load Theory concerns new information: working memory limits apply to what students have not yet learned, and long-term memory removes the bottleneck.
Element interactivity, the number of parts that must be held in mind together, drives both intrinsic and extraneous load, and it depends on prior knowledge.
The same strategy can help in one lesson and not another; worked examples help novices with complex content but make little difference with simple content or knowledgeable students.
The aim is to cut wasted effort while keeping the thinking learning requires, not to minimise load at all times.
The five planning steps are check prior knowledge, find high-interactivity moments, match guidance, cut extraneous load, and fade support.
quotes: Cognitive Load Theory is John Sweller's theory of how we learn knowledge that needs to be explicitly taught.
Long-term memory has no known limits. Once knowledge is stored there, working memory can draw on it freely, and the bottleneck disappears.

Their advantage wasn't a bigger working memory. It was knowledge: familiar configurations stored in long-term memory allowed them to process many individual pieces as a small number of meaningful patterns.

So the useful takeaway from CLT is to manage complexity in relation to what students already know. Strip out demands that don't contribute to learning, provide more support when students are dealing with unfamiliar, complex content, then gradually remove that support as their knowledge grows.
If most of the class can't recall it, the new material will be far more demanding than you planned for. Secure the foundation first.
For novices learning complex content, give a clear explanation and a worked example before they try a similar problem alone.
Independent practice should make skills automatic, so working memory is free for harder thinking. Check understanding with whole-class responses before removing anything.
What looks like one piece of information to an expert may be many interacting elements to a novice.
